lines.note: This Portuguese continuation says that something is in a full house; the referent belongs to the entry on the preceding page. No new Japanese headword begins here.
Manzai is equated with mannen, many or thousands of years. The two Japanese forms are upright, unlike the Portuguese explanation continuing below.
De annos completes the preceding gloss. Manzairacu introduces the pleasure or felicity associated with longevity; the abbreviated and divided Contentamẽ- continues on the next physical row.

runs.text: tos de vida de muitos annos.

lines.note: Completes contentamentos as the pleasures of a life lasting many years. This is a continuation of Manzairacu, not a separate entry.

runs.text: Official vniuerſal que faz todo ge-

lines.note: Manzaicu denotes a versatile artisan who performs every kind of manual work. The scan supports vniuerſal, correcting the OCR's intrusive o; genero remains divided at the printed hyphen.
Nero completes genero, and obra de mãos specifies manual craftsmanship. The tilde remains on the printed a rather than being moved to the following vowel.
Manzǒ names all visible things. The example begins Xin- and continues as Xinra manzǒ below; the caron is visible over the long vowel.
Completes Xinra manzǒ, the totality of phenomena, with Idem referring back to the preceding definition. Preserve the physical division within Xinra.

runs.text: Eſtar cheo, farto, ou ſatiſfeito. Vt,

lines.note: Manzocu means being full, sated, or satisfied. Cheo is the historical Portuguese spelling visible in the scan, not the OCR's obeo; the example follows below.
Manzocu xita expresses satisfaction, glossed as being content and satisfied. The scan supplies the missing t in ſatiſfeito; the abbreviation in cõtente is retained.

runs.text: ¶ Item, He palaura cõque hũ moſtra alegrar-

lines.note: The entry adds a pragmatic use: a word by which someone shows gladness. Alegrar- is visibly divided, and the reflexive continuation belongs to the next row.
Completes alegrar-se and adds thanking someone for something. This explains the social use of Manzocu rather than introducing a new Japanese expression.

runs.text: Conuidar a dez mil Bonzos co-

lines.note: Manzôcuyǒ is an offering ceremony inviting ten thousand Buddhist monks. The scan has capital Bonzos, not honzos; the first long-o mark is a circumflex and the final one a caron.

runs.text: mo ſe faz em algũas grandes exequias, & dar

lines.note: Completes como and places the ceremony at large funeral observances. Dar begins the further action of giving alms, completed on the following line.
Lhes eſmola completes the instruction to give the invited monks alms. There is no visible hyphen after dar on the preceding row to supply retrospectively.
Mappajime is the very beginning. Qiǒno map- starts an example about the beginning of a book; the Japanese compound is physically divided here.
Completes mappajimeni atta: it was at the beginning of the book. The Portuguese Eſtaua gives the past location rather than a command or definition of a new noun.
Mappira is an emphatic adverb, glossed as in any case or by all means. The repeated example begins Map-, not OCR Man-, as the descending p is visible.
The example asks emphatically for forgiveness; yuruite is a historical form and is not modernized. Xid. is an upright citation label, while the Portuguese Diſ- begins the translation.

runs.text: ſe que lhe perdoaße em todas as maneiras.

lines.note: Completes Diſſe: he said to forgive him by all means. The scan joins perdoaße into one word; the printed double-s sort is retained rather than modernizing the subjunctive.
Mappiru is midday. The emphatic initial geminate is present in Japanese, while Portuguese uses the historical spelling Meo dia.
Mappô is paraphrased as Suyeno nori, the final law or teaching. The Buddhist sense is explained by the following Portuguese clause; the abbreviation q̃ remains unexpanded.
Veo no fim completes the description of the teaching that came at the end. The short row belongs to Mappô and retains the historical Portuguese verb form.
Mapponajiyǒni means in precisely the same manner. Adu. is italic grammatical apparatus, and the Portuguese maneira is divided after manei-.
Ra completes maneira; pontualmente emphasizes exact correspondence. This continuation finishes the adverbial definition begun on the preceding row.

runs.text: Meo, ou centro dalgũa couſa re-

lines.note: Mappucura denotes the middle or centre of something round. Redonda is divided after re-, and the next rows add a temporal or figurative sense.

runs.text: donda. ¶ Item, Tempo em que florece al-

lines.note: After completing redonda, the entry adds the time when something flourishes. Algũa is divided across the line boundary, so al- is not a separate word.

runs.text: gũa couſa, ou he aforça, & vigor della.

lines.note: The figurative sense is the flourishing time, strength, or vigour of something. The scan supports he, the historical copula, rather than OCR be; the close spacing in aforça is retained.
Maqe here names an eye disease, distinct from the following verb meaning to lose. Maqeuo starts an example whose verb appears below.
Maqeuo vazzurǒ means suffering from the eye complaint. The doubled z and final caron belong to the historical Japanese spelling and agree with the Portuguese gloss.
The principal forms introduce the verb for being defeated or losing. The Portuguese lists a game, dispute, and battle, with disputa divided at the visible hyphen.
Ta completes disputa, followed by pelleja, battle. The physical continuation completes the circumstances in which the verb Maqe is used.

runs.text: O ſer vẽcido, ou perder no jogo, &c.

lines.note: This separate nominal Maqe denotes defeat or losing at a game. Its definition should not be merged with the preceding verbal principal parts.
Maqei is explained by Tenguno facaricoto, a tengu's stratagem, translated in the dictionary's Christian vocabulary as the devil's cunning. Facaricoto is Japanese, not part of the Portuguese sentence.
Maqeiuo yôjin xeyo tells the reader to beware of such stratagems. The Portuguese imperative begins Vi- and continues below; the circumflex in yôjin is retained.

runs.text: giai vos dos ardijs do demonio.

lines.note: Completes Vigiai vos dos ardijs do demonio, a warning against the demon's wiles. Ardijs is the visible historical spelling, not modernized to ardis.
Maqe icuſa is a battle in which one has been defeated. The compound is printed with a space, and naqual is retained as the closely set Portuguese form.
This Maqi means a demonic being, paraphrased by Tengu voni. The Portuguese Diabo is the dictionary's gloss and should not collapse this entry into the following homonymous pasture term.

runs.text: Lugar onde ſe crião caualos brauos.

lines.note: Maqi here denotes a place where untamed horses are bred. The following example identifies a horse from such a pasture, not another meaning of the preceding demonic term.
Maqino vma and maqidaxi are alternative names for an untamed horse. The visible paragraph sign is restored; l is the dictionary's Latin alternative marker, not the numeral one.
Bravo, ou do mato completes the description of a wild or woodland horse. This indented continuation belongs to the example on the preceding row.
A separate Maqi names a tree suitable for timber. The broad botanical description does not by itself identify a modern species.
Maqi, with the forms u and aita, means rolling up or wrapping. The Portuguese emburulhar is preserved in its printed historical spelling.
Xitauo maqu is the idiom for astonishment, literally involving the tongue. The next example begins Xirouo, with object particle uo, not OCR Xirono; its verb follows below.
Xirouo maqu means surrounding a fortress. The new example begins Vxiro- and continues into maqiuo ſuru on the next physical line.

runs.text: Dar nos inimigos por de tras,

lines.note: Completes Vxiromaqiuo ſuru, attacking an enemy from behind. The Portuguese explanation continues below and across the column boundary.

runs.text: ou nas coſtas como quando tem de cerco a forta-

lines.note: The attack is against the enemy's rear, for example while they are besieging a fortress. The scan resolves the severely garbled OCR as ou nas coſtas como quando tem de cerco a forta-; fortaleza continues in column 2.
Leza completes fortaleza across the column boundary. Iqiga maqu then illustrates panting or catching one's breath; Reſfole- begins the Portuguese verb continued below.

runs.text: gar afadigado como quando hum correo, ou ſu-

lines.note: The breathing is laboured, as after running. The Portuguese continues with another exertion, climbing a slope, divided after ſu-.
Bio completes ſubio ladeira, climbing a hill. Vzzugamaqu introduces the swirling or seething motion of a whirlpool; keep the printed lack of internal spacing.
The whirlpools are specifically of water. Vzzuno maqu- begins the longer quoted Japanese illustration of being carried round with the waves.

runs.text: ni xitagaite namito tomoni meguru coto

lines.note: The quotation describes going round together with the waves according to the whirlpool's motion. The scan separates ni from xitagaite; the row is entirely Japanese.

runs.text: chauſuuo voſu yorimo ſumiyaca nari. Tai-

lines.note: The motion is faster than pushing a tea mill. Tai- begins the divided source label, not part of the preceding Japanese syntax; preserve the printed voſu spelling.

runs.text: Lib. 18. O ir às voltas com as on-

lines.note: Feiq. completes the upright Taifeiq. citation, followed by italic book number and translation. The Portuguese begins going round with the waves and divides ondas after on-.

runs.text: das conforme ao rolheiro, era mais de preſſa do q̃

lines.note: Completes ondas and compares the speed of the whirlpool-driven motion with the mill. The visible abbreviation q̃ is retained and separated from do as printed.

runs.text: a mò do cha ſe moue.

lines.note: The translation ends with the movement of the tea millstone. The scan has lowercase italic cha within the Portuguese sentence, not the OCR's capitalized Cha; mò retains its grave.
This nominal Maqi is rolling up or wrapping. Migui- starts the term for rightward winding, whose explanation occupies the following rows.

runs.text: O enrolar às direitas. i, Com a mão

lines.note: Completes Miguimaqi, rightward winding. The visible word is direitas, not OCR dircitas; the hand movement defining this direction is continued below.
Rightward winding moves the hand toward the body. Fidari maqi introduces the opposite direction; the Portuguese article at the right edge is visibly capital O.

runs.text: contrario. i, O enrolar meneando a mão pera

lines.note: The opposite winding direction is defined by moving the hand outward. The scan reads meneando, moving, rather than the OCR's mencando.
A parte de fora completes the outward-hand movement defining Fidari maqi. This short continuation closes the directional contrast.
A homonymous Maqi means sowing. It has the same listed principal endings as the wrapping verb but a separate Portuguese definition.
Maqiague means raising something by rolling it up. Its principal forms are followed by a concrete example involving hanging blinds.
Sudareuo tacaqu maqiaguru illustrates rolling blinds up high. The compound remains maqiaguru, not a contracted modernized spelling; Ale- begins the translation.

runs.text: uantar em alto as esteiras que eſtão dependura-

lines.note: Completes aleuantar and describes lifting the hanging mats or blinds. The adjective dependuradas is divided at the right edge and continued below.
Das completes dependuradas; enrolandoas specifies that the blinds are raised by rolling them. The object pronoun remains attached to the gerund as printed.
Maqiauaxe describes involving someone along with other people. The scan supports no, not OCR mo; retain the printed principal part ſuru rather than regularizing it from a modern paradigm.

runs.text: numero de outros, ou à volta de outros ainda

lines.note: The person is included among, or swept along with, others. The Portuguese continues with a qualification about lack of culpability.
The person may be innocent. Maqiauaxeni vǒ is the example of suffering such involvement; the scan ends it with a full stop, not the OCR's hyphen.

runs.text: A certar de ir à volta de outros na execução de

lines.note: The translation describes happening to be included with others when a punishment is carried out. The conspicuous separation in printed A certar is retained rather than normalized into the modern word.

runs.text: algum caſtigo, ou justiça ainda que não tenha

lines.note: The collective treatment is punishment or an act of justice even where the individual is not guilty. Caſtigo corrects the OCR's cafigo; the final qualification continues below.
Culpa completes the statement that the person has no fault. This very short continuation closes the Maqiauaxe example and is not an omitted independent entry.

Maqibaxira is a decorated pillar, here described with several colours and gold ornament. The scan gives baxira, not OCR baxita, and the second pass confirms Columna with m, not Colunna. Pinturas is divided without a visible terminal hyphen after pin.
Turas completes pinturas de ouro, gold decoration. Preserve the physical division without inventing a hyphen on the preceding row.
Maqicacuxi means hiding something by rolling it up. The Portuguese begins Enrolando, not OCR Eurolando; the historical aita principal part is retained.
Fatajiruxiuo maqicacuſu illustrates concealing a banner. The Japanese object is upright, and Eſconder begins the Portuguese explanation continued below.
The banner is hidden by rolling it up. The attached object ending in enrolandoa is retained as printed, without modern punctuation or a hyphen.
Maqicayexi means rolling back or rolling up again. The scan reads Tornar a enrolar, correcting both OCR consonant errors; retain the clearly printed eita principal part.
The example rolls from the edge toward the inner end, then back toward the edge. Faxi at the right boundary continues syntactically with ni on the next row, without a printed hyphen.
Ni maqicayeſu completes the reverse-rolling action. The Portuguese identifies the object as a letter or written sheet, rather than adding a Japanese headword.

runs.text: eſcrito atè o cabo, & do cabo tornar a enrolar

lines.note: The paper is rolled as far as its end and then rolled back from that end. Atè retains its printed grave accent; the destination of the return movement follows below.
Atè o principio completes the instruction to roll back to the beginning. This continuation closes Maqicayexi before the separate scattering verb.
Maqichiraxi means scattering while sowing. Its Japanese principal forms agree with the Portuguese Semeando eſpalhar and lead into examples below.
Taneuo maqichiraſu illustrates sowing seed by scattering it. Eſpalhando is divided without a visible hyphen after eſpalhan, which is not silently supplied.
Do completes eſpalhando a ſemente. Per met. introduces a metaphorical example of scattering gold and silver; the Japanese verb is divided after ma-.
Completes maqichiraſu in the example about gold and silver. The Portuguese reads eſpalhar, scatter, not the OCR's eſtahar; the final object continues below.
Prata completes the paired objects gold and silver. This indented continuation belongs to the metaphorical scattering example, not the following wrapping verb.
Maqicome means putting something inside by wrapping it. The scan resolves the OCR noise as Emburulhando meter dentro; the entry prints only the two listed principal forms here.
Como na carta gives a letter as an example of the wrapping or enclosure just defined. The row is an indented continuation, not a separate headword.
Maqicomi means drawing or rolling something inward. Enrolando corrects OCR Eurolando, and the printed past ending ôda retains its circumflex.
The definition adds swallowing or engulfing. Vzzuga funeuo ma- begins the example in which a whirlpool draws in a boat; the verb continues below.

runs.text: O rolheiro ſorueo a Fune enuolta cõ

lines.note: Completes maqicomu: the whirlpool engulfed the boat among the waves. The printed Fune is a Japanese boat-word embedded in the Portuguese translation and is retained in its visible italic type.
As ondas completes the phrase about the boat being swept in with the waves. This continuation ends Maqicomi before the following turning verb.

The scan clearly gives Maqifirugayexi, turning by rolling, rather than the badly corrupted OCR headword. The principal ending is eita; the example continues on the next page, anticipated by the bottom catchword.
